final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

**The short version:**
1. **Hire or DIY? Both, but split deliberately.** Do the daily work yourself; buy the one thing you can't manufacture alone — a dog that appears at a distance you choose. That's a reactive-dog group class, not a $2,400 private program. Nothing in this dog's presentation (barking, no bite, still physically manageable) justifies the premium tier yet, and escalating later is easy.
2. **Three options, real prices:** The Hound Haven, Santa Clara — **$470** for both Growly Dog classes (best value, but their published schedule is stale, needs a call). D For Dogz — **$595** group class, Saturday mornings + Wednesday evening Zoom (best fit for evenings/weekends). Stacy's Wag'N'Train — **$1,500** for the matching package, most credentialed, but her listing says weekdays-daytime only, so probably a non-starter. I excluded the e-collar outfits and explained why in the report.
3. **Four weeks** built on the Engage-Disengage Game from Karen Pryor Clicker Training, plus 300-Peck for the pulling. Week 1 is deliberately *no* dog exposure — management and mechanics only. Each week is its own subtask with the full protocol in the description.

**Two judgement calls I made, flag if you disagree:**
- I treated the pulling and the barking as one problem, not two. Leash tension raises arousal and lowers the reactivity threshold, so fixing the leash makes the reactivity work easier.
- I assumed no bite history, since you didn't mention one. If he has ever bitten or injured a dog or person, the recommendation changes — skip the class and go straight to a private consult or a vet behaviourist.

**Your next moves, in order:** buy the kit → call The Hound Haven on 650-224-7707 → start Week 1 without waiting for the class to begin. Six open subtasks, all yours: one errand, three calls/emails, and the four week-blocks.

Setting to needs_review — nothing is blocked, I just want you to sanity-check the hire-vs-DIY call before you spend anything.

report.markdown:
# Training plan: 14-month rescue border collie mix — pulling + barking at dogs

**Bottom line:** Start the daily work yourself this week. Buy exactly one thing from a professional — controlled practice with a decoy dog — which means a reactive-dog group class at **$470–$595**, not a $2,400 private program. Total first-month spend: **under $700**, including equipment.

---

## 1. Hire a trainer, or do it yourself?

**Both, split deliberately.** You do the daily mechanics; you pay for the one thing you cannot manufacture alone.

### The thing you can't do by yourself
Every credible protocol for this problem requires working **under threshold** — close enough that he notices another dog, far enough that he can still think. <cite index="106-1">Under threshold means the dog is far enough away that they can notice the trigger but not "lose their brain"</cite>. On a public street you have no control over that distance: a dog comes round the corner at 15 feet and the session is over. A reactive-dog class is, functionally, rental of controlled trigger distance plus a second pair of eyes on your timing.

This matters because <cite index="112-5">every time your dog practises an undesired behaviour outside of training time, he is going backward in training</cite>. The ratio of controlled reps to ambush reps is the whole game.

### Why not the $2,400+ private program
Nothing here justifies it yet. Barking with no reported bite, no injury, and a handler who can still physically manage the dog is the ordinary, good-prognosis version of this problem. And in day-training formats the trainer works the dog — but the behaviour has to hold on *your* walks with *you* on the leash. For reactivity, handler skill is the actual deliverable, so coaching beats done-for-you. Escalating later is easy; un-spending $2,400 is not.

### Why the DIY half is realistic
- **It's barking, not biting.** <cite index="112-1">The Engage-Disengage Game is designed for dogs that respond with a "fight" or "fool around" response</cite> — barking and lunging sit squarely in that category. The mechanic is simple: notice dog → click → treat.
- **14 months is the normal onset window,** and the behaviour is young. <cite index="107-1">The sooner reactive behaviour is addressed, the better the prognosis</cite>.
- **Evenings and weekends is enough.** This needs 5–15 minutes a day, not hours.

### What makes this dog harder than average
| Factor | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Barks at *every* dog | Low threshold; no easy wins available on normal walks |
| Pulling + reactivity together | Leash tension raises arousal, which lowers the threshold. Fixing the leash makes the reactivity work easier — not separate projects |
| Border collie mix | Motion-sensitive, high-arousal; under-met mental needs surface as reactivity |
| Rescue, unknown history | You don't know what's already been rehearsed |

On the breed: guidance puts a collie's requirement at <cite index="117-1">at least thirty minutes to an hour of dedicated mental work every single day, on top of physical exercise, not as a replacement for it</cite>. And the specific trap to avoid is trying to <cite index="116-0">"exercise the problem away"</cite> — an under-worked collie that gets more running just becomes a fitter, more aroused collie.

### Tripwires — stop DIY and hire properly if any of these appear
1. **Any bite or injury.** <cite index="112-6">If your dog has bitten or caused injury, first consult a certified positive reinforcement trainer or board-certified veterinary behaviourist</cite>.
2. Lunging you can't physically hold.
3. Zero improvement after 4–6 weeks of consistent work.
4. Reactivity generalising — off-leash, through windows, toward people.
5. He can't recover: stays wound up for the rest of the walk, or stops taking food outdoors entirely.

---

## 2. Local options with real prices

All three are force-free. All prices were taken from each business's own site on 4 Aug 2026 — not from aggregator estimates.

### ⭐ Option A — The Hound Haven (best value; start here)
Peggy McCarty, CTC (SF SPCA Academy for Dog Trainers)
📍 2200 Lafayette St, Unit 1, Santa Clara · ☎ 650-224-7707 · peggy@thehoundhaven.com

| Service | Price |
|---|---|
| Growly Dog **Foundation** — 3 weeks, 50 min/session *(prerequisite)* | **$160** |
| Growly Dog — 5-week small group, 50 min/session | **$310** |
| **Both classes** | **$470** |
| Private in-home: 90-min consult + eval | $160 |
| Private session thereafter | $125/hr (package discount available) |
| Remote phone/video consult | $55 / 30 min · $100 / 60 min |

<cite index="129-1">The class is explicitly for dogs that bark, lunge and pull on leash</cite> — precisely this dog. <cite index="129-0">The 3-week foundation is required before the 5-week class</cite>.

⚠️ **The published schedule is stale** (shows Feb/Mar/Apr, Tuesdays 4:30pm and 5:40pm). Call for current dates and confirm an evening slot.

### Option B — D For Dogz (most structured; best schedule fit)
Kaajal Tiwary, Victoria Stilwell Academy mentor · ☎ 650-538-3011 · free 15-min discovery call bookable online
Serves <cite index="126-0">San Jose, Willow Glen, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Milpitas, Campbell, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Los Altos, Cupertino, Mountain View, Palo Alto</cite>

| Service | Price |
|---|---|
| **Leash Reactive Dog Foundations group class** — <cite index="130-0">9 sessions over 5 weeks</cite> | **$595** |
| "Reactive to Distinguished Dogs" follow-on (real-world outings) | $500/month |
| Private Coaching, 6 weeks (you train, she coaches) | $2,400 |
| Day Training, 6 weeks (trainer works the dog) | $4,200 |

Group class runs <cite index="130-1">in-person Saturdays 9:30–10:30 AM plus a live Zoom Q&A Wednesdays 6:30–7:15 PM</cite>, and <cite index="130-2">the first two in-person sessions are people-only</cite>. That schedule fits an evenings-and-weekends owner exactly. In-person sessions are in Palo Alto — confirm the drive is acceptable. <cite index="131-0">$420 off for enrolling in the full program.</cite>

### Option C — Stacy's Wag'N'Train (most credentialed; scheduling risk)
Stacy Braslau-Schneck, MA, CPDT-KA, CBCC-KA — 25+ years, San Jose · stacy@wagntrain.com

| Service | Price |
|---|---|
| <cite index="122-2">Behavior Consultation/Evaluation — ~1 hour</cite> | <cite index="122-2">$190, or included in any package</cite> |
| Basic 4-pack (4 × 1hr) | $800 |
| **Beginning Behavior Modification 6-pack** ← matching tier | **$1,500** |
| Behavior Mod Foundation (14 × 1hr) | $3,000 |
| Virtual only | <cite index="121-0">$145/hr; $580 for four basic lessons; $870 for six lessons for aggression or serious issues</cite> |
| Post-package single sessions | $130 |

⚠️ Her Yelp listing states <cite index="123-0">private lesson appointments are available on weekdays during the daytime</cite> and that she's <cite index="123-0">often booked 1–3 weeks in advance</cite>. That probably rules out in-person unless the $870 virtual package can run in the evening. Worth an email, low priority.

### Deliberately excluded
- **Off Leash K9 San Jose** (<cite index="115-0">$500 first lesson including e-collar, then $100/session</cite>) and **Sit Means Sit** — e-collar based. This dog's barking is almost certainly fear or frustration driven, and <cite index="118-0">study after study shows that when punishment and aversive training are used on aggressive dogs, the first side effect is increased aggression</cite>. Adding pain in the presence of another dog risks converting barking into biting.
- **Humane Society Silicon Valley** — cheap classes (<cite index="124-0">Beginning and Intermediate Obedience $150 for six sessions</cite>) but <cite index="125-0">they do not currently offer private training or consultation to the general public</cite>, and their loose-leash workshop <cite index="119-0">explicitly excludes leash-reactive and dog-aggressive dogs</cite>.
- **The Hound Haven's standard group classes** ($280/5wk) also <cite index="128-0">exclude dogs who bark, pull, lunge or growl at other dogs on leash</cite> — the Growly Dog track is the right door there.

---

## 3. The four-week plan

Core protocol: the **Engage-Disengage Game** (Alice Tong, KPA CTP / Karen Pryor Clicker Training), plus **300-Peck** for loose-leash walking. Each week has its own subtask in the tree.

### The rule underneath all four weeks
Split your walks in two. **Training walks** are short, deliberate, under threshold. **Exercise walks** are routed and timed to avoid dogs entirely — early morning, late evening, industrial streets, or drive somewhere empty. Never both on the same outing.

### Equipment (~$60–$120)
Front-clip or Y-front harness (Freedom No-Pull, Balance, Perfect Fit) · standard **6 ft** leash, **never retractable** · 15–30 ft long line · belt-mounted treat pouch · clicker or a consistent marker word · pea-sized high-value treats — chicken, cheese, hot dog. Kibble will not compete with the sight of another dog.

### Week 1 — Management + three mechanics. **Zero deliberate dog exposure.**
Re-route every walk to avoid dogs. Then, indoors or in the driveway, 5 min twice a day:
1. **Charge the marker** — click, feed, 20 reps.
2. **Emergency U-turn** — "let's go!", lure a fast 180, feed. 10 reps/day until it's automatic *for you*. This is your entire safety net for weeks 2–4. Build on the protocol's own advice to <cite index="112-9">practise fast U-turns by luring with a treat at the nose or tossing "find it" treats on the ground as you change direction</cite>.
3. **"Find it" scatter** — toss 3–5 treats on the ground to defuse a moment.

**Loose leash (300-Peck):** reward every single step with a loose leash; then every 2, 3, 4, building up. Any pull resets the count to 1. Feed at your knee on the side he's walking. Separately adopt "be a tree" — stop dead on tension, move only when it slackens.

*Move on when:* the U-turn is fluent, he responds to the marker, and you get 4–5 loose-leash steps on a quiet street.

### Week 2 — Engage-Disengage **Level 1**
Find a spot where dogs pass predictably at 100+ ft. Find the **threshold distance** — where he notices but doesn't bark — and write the number down. That number is your metric for the month.

<cite index="112-11">Start at a safe distance where your dog is not reacting; be quiet and still so he notices the trigger on his own. At the precise moment he engages by looking at the trigger, click. When he turns his head toward you after the click, feed him. If he reacts or doesn't turn back, move further away and reset at an easier distance.</cite>

<cite index="112-12">Goal: at least 3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before moving to Level 2 — a success is when he turns back to you immediately after the click.</cite> <cite index="112-19">Play for 1–5 minutes, then take a break.</cite> <cite index="112-10">Stop if you notice subtle stress signals such as excessive lip-licking, yawning, or scratching.</cite>

### Week 3 — Engage-Disengage **Level 2**, and close the distance
<cite index="112-15">Let him notice the trigger, but this time wait 1–5 seconds to see if he'll offer to look away on his own; if he fixates for longer than 5 seconds, go back to Level 1. At the precise moment he disengages by looking away, click, then feed.</cite>

<cite index="112-18">Goal: 3–5 successful reps in a row before moving 1–5 steps closer.</cite> Only a few steps — this is the week people rush and lose the month. And: <cite index="112-13">if the trigger is moving or changing in intensity, keep playing Level 1</cite> at each new distance.

Why Level 2 is the real prize: <cite index="112-8">the second level rewards the alternative behaviour of turning away from the trigger — a behaviour incompatible with barking at, pulling toward, or biting the trigger</cite>.

On real walks, your response to a surprise dog is U-turn or "find it", then leave. Don't train through ambushes.

### Week 4 — Moving dogs, parallel passes, honest assessment
Moving dogs are much harder than static ones — drop back to Level 1 at a longer distance. That's expected, not regression.

**Parallel passes:** if you can borrow a friend with a calm dog, walk the same direction on opposite sides of a wide street at threshold distance, clicking and feeding throughout. **No greetings.** This is the highest-value exercise of the month — and it's exactly what a class supplies on tap.

**Realistic 4-week target:** pass a dog on the far side of a normal residential street, no bark, loose leash, taking food throughout. *Not* expected yet: same-pavement passes, handling a barking dog coming at you, or anything at a dog park.

### What to avoid all four weeks
Prong / choke / e-collars · punishing the bark (it's the warning — suppress it and you may lose the warning without changing the feeling) · flooding: dog parks, busy trails, "let him say hi" · tight leash near a trigger · trying to exercise the problem away.

### Running alongside: the collie baseline
Feed every meal from a snuffle mat or puzzle instead of a bowl · 10 min/day trick or scent work · long-line decompression sniff walks somewhere empty. A 20-minute sniff walk does more for his threshold than a five-mile run.

---

## Recommended sequence
1. Buy the kit this week (~$60–$120).
2. Call **The Hound Haven, 650-224-7707** for current Growly Dog dates → **$470** if the timing works.
3. If it doesn't, book the free discovery call with **D For Dogz, 650-538-3011** → **$595**, Saturday mornings + Wednesday evening Zoom.
4. Start Week 1 immediately — don't wait for the class to begin.
5. Reassess at week 4 against the tripwires.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
DONE. ANSWER: Do both — but not in the way most people mean. Do the daily work yourself starting this week, and buy ONE thing from a professional: access to controlled setups with a decoy dog. That means a reactive-dog group class ($470–$595), not a $2,400 private program.

WHY NOT PURE DIY:
The single thing an owner cannot manufacture alone is a dog that appears at a chosen distance and stays there. Every protocol for leash reactivity (Engage-Disengage, LAT, BAT) depends on working "under threshold" — close enough that the dog notices the other dog, far enough that it can still think. On a public street you get no say: a dog rounds the corner at 15 feet and your session is over. A reactive-dog class is essentially a rental of controlled trigger distance, plus a second pair of eyes on your timing. The Karen Pryor Engage-Disengage write-up is blunt that every reaction outside training time is backward progress — so the ratio of controlled reps to ambush reps is the whole game.

WHY NOT FULL PRIVATE / DAY TRAINING:
Nothing in this dog's presentation justifies $2,400–$4,200 yet. Barking at other dogs with no reported bite, no reported injury, and a handler who can still physically manage the dog is the ordinary, good-prognosis version of this problem. Also, in day-training programs the trainer works the dog — but the behaviour has to hold on YOUR walks, with YOU on the end of the leash. For reactivity specifically, handler skill is the deliverable, so the coaching format is a better buy than the done-for-you format.

WHY THE DIY HALF IS REALISTIC HERE:
- Barking, not biting. Fight-type/frustration reactivity is exactly what Engage-Disengage is designed for and it's mechanically simple: notice trigger → click → treat.
- 14 months is adolescence — this is the normal onset window, the behaviour is young, and prognosis is best when addressed early rather than after years of rehearsal.
- Evenings and weekends is enough time. This needs 5–15 minutes a day, not hours.

WHAT MAKES THIS DOG HARDER THAN AVERAGE (arguing for the class, not against DIY):
- "Every other dog" = low threshold and no easy wins available on ordinary walks.
- Two problems interacting: pulling puts constant leash tension on the dog, and tension itself raises arousal, which lowers the reactivity threshold. Fixing the leash makes the reactivity work easier — they are not separate projects.
- Border collie mix: motion-sensitive, high-arousal, and a breed where under-met mental needs reliably show up as reactivity. Guidance for the breed puts dedicated mental work at 30–60 min/day ON TOP of physical exercise, and warns against trying to exercise the problem away — an under-worked collie that gets more running just gets fitter and more aroused.
- Rescue with unknown history: you don't know what's already been rehearsed or what happened to it.

TRIPWIRES — stop DIY and hire a private behaviour consultant or a veterinary behaviourist immediately if ANY of these appear:
1. Any bite or injury to a dog or person (the Karen Pryor protocol says consult a certified professional first in this case).
2. Lunging you cannot physically hold, or you get pulled off your feet.
3. Zero improvement after 4–6 weeks of consistent daily work.
4. Reactivity generalising — starts happening off-leash, through windows, or toward people.
5. The dog can't recover: stays wound up for the rest of the walk after one incident (trigger stacking), or stops taking food outdoors at all.

BUDGET FRAMING: the DIY half costs roughly $60–$120 in equipment. The class half is $470 (The Hound Haven) or $595 (D For Dogz). Total under $700 versus $2,400+ for a private program — and you can always escalate later. Escalating is easy; un-spending $2,400 is not.

subtasks.description:
DONE. Plan built on the Engage-Disengage Game (Alice Tong, KPA CTP, published by Karen Pryor Clicker Training) as the core reactivity protocol, with the 300-Peck method for loose-leash walking. Full week-by-week detail is in the report attached to the parent task; each week also has its own subtask.

CORE MECHANIC — Engage-Disengage, exact protocol as published:
Level 1 (ENGAGE): Stand at a distance where the dog notices the other dog but does not react. Stay quiet and still, let him notice it on his own. The moment he LOOKS at the other dog, CLICK. When he turns back to you after the click, feed. If he reacts or doesn't turn back, you are too close — move further away. Goal: 3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before advancing.
Level 2 (DISENGAGE): Let him notice the trigger, then wait 1–5 seconds to see if he looks away on his own. If he stares longer than 5 seconds, drop back to Level 1. The instant he DISENGAGES, CLICK, then feed. Goal: 3–5 successful reps in a row, then move 1–5 steps closer.
Rules that matter: play 1–5 minutes then take a break. If the trigger is moving or changing intensity, go back to Level 1 at the new distance. Stop on subtle stress signals — lip-licking, yawning, scratching.
Why it works: Level 1 builds a positive association with the sight of other dogs; Level 2 trains turning away, which is physically incompatible with barking and lunging.

THE MANAGEMENT RULE THAT UNDERPINS ALL FOUR WEEKS:
Every reaction outside of training time is backward progress. So for these four weeks, walks are split in two: TRAINING walks (deliberate, short, under threshold) and GETTING-THE-DOG-EXERCISED walks (routed and timed to avoid dogs entirely — early morning, late evening, industrial streets, or drive to an empty space). Do not try to do both on the same outing.

EQUIPMENT (~$60–$120 total):
- Front-clip or Y-front harness (Freedom No-Pull, Balance Harness, Perfect Fit). Redirects pulling without choking. A head halter (Gentle Leader) is the fallback if you can't physically hold him — introduce it gradually with food.
- Standard 6 ft leash. NOT retractable — retractables teach that pulling produces forward movement, which is the exact opposite of this plan.
- 15–30 ft long line for decompression sniff walks in open space.
- Treat pouch worn on the belt. Fumbling in a pocket destroys your timing.
- Clicker, or a consistent marker word ("yes"). Either is fine; consistency is what counts.
- High-value soft treats cut pea-sized: chicken, cheese, hot dog. Kibble will not compete with the sight of another dog.
- Snuffle mat or puzzle feeder for the enrichment baseline.

WHAT TO AVOID FOR THE FULL FOUR WEEKS:
- Prong, choke and e-collars. Aversives applied in the presence of another dog risk the dog pairing the pain with the other dog, escalating barking into biting. Multiple sources link aversive tools to increased fear, anxiety and aggression.
- Punishing or correcting the bark. The bark is the warning; suppress it and you may lose the warning without changing the underlying feeling.
- Flooding: dog parks, busy trails, "let him say hi to get used to it." On-leash greetings with an already-reactive dog make it worse.
- Tight leash near a trigger. Tension raises arousal and lowers the threshold. Keep a J-shaped slack line even when nervous.
- Trying to exercise the problem away. Running a border collie more just produces a fitter, more aroused border collie.

BORDER COLLIE BASELINE (runs alongside all four weeks, non-negotiable):
Breed guidance puts a collie's need at 30–60 min/day of dedicated MENTAL work, on top of physical exercise, not instead of it. An under-worked adolescent collie has a lower reactivity threshold on every walk. Cheapest version: feed every meal out of a snuffle mat or puzzle instead of a bowl, 10 min/day of trick or scent training (hide treats in boxes, "find it" around the house), and one long-line decompression sniff walk somewhere empty a few times a week. Sniffing is genuinely calming — a 20-minute sniff walk does more for the threshold than a 5-mile run.

subtasks.title: Buy the kit: front-clip harness, 6ft leash, long line, treat pouch, clicker
subtasks.description:
Do this before Week 1 starts. Roughly $60-$120 total.

- Front-clip / Y-front harness: Freedom No-Pull, Balance Harness, or Perfect Fit. Measure the chest before ordering.
- Standard 6 ft leash. NOT retractable.
- 15-30 ft long line (biothane is easiest to handle) for decompression sniff walks.
- Treat pouch that clips to the belt - fumbling in a pocket wrecks your timing on the click.
- Clicker (or just commit to a marker word, 'yes').
- High-value soft treats: chicken, cheese, or hot dog, cut pea-sized. Kibble will not beat the sight of another dog.
- Snuffle mat or puzzle feeder for meals.

Available same-day at most Bay Area pet stores; harness fit is worth trying on in person.

subtasks.title: Week 1: management + three mechanics, ZERO deliberate dog exposure
subtasks.description:
GOAL THIS WEEK: stop the rehearsal, and build the three mechanical skills in an environment with no other dogs. You are not doing reactivity training this week. Resist the urge.

MANAGEMENT (all week):
- Re-route and re-time every walk to avoid dogs. Early morning, late evening, quiet or industrial streets, or drive somewhere empty. Every bark he doesn't get to practise is a win.
- If a dog appears anyway: emergency U-turn and leave. Do not try to train through it.

THREE MECHANICS - practise indoors / in the driveway, 5 min twice a day:
1. CHARGE THE MARKER. Click (or say 'yes'), then immediately feed. 20 reps. He should start looking to you at the sound.
2. EMERGENCY U-TURN. Say 'let's go!', lure a fast 180 with a treat at his nose, feed as you move away. 10 reps a day until it's automatic FOR YOU. This is your entire safety net for weeks 2-4.
3. 'FIND IT' SCATTER. Say 'find it', toss 3-5 treats on the ground. This gets his nose down and defuses a moment. 10 reps.

LOOSE LEASH (300-Peck method), driveway then a quiet street, 5-10 min/day:
Reward every single step taken with a loose leash. When that's easy, reward every 2 steps, then 3, then 4, building up. The rule: any time he pulls, reset the count back to 1. Feed at your knee on the side he's walking, so he isn't lured across your body. Separately, adopt the 'be a tree' rule on ordinary walks - the second the leash goes tight you stop dead, and you only move again when it slackens.

ENRICHMENT: all meals out of a snuffle mat or puzzle feeder starting now. One long-line sniff walk in an open empty space.

READY FOR WEEK 2 WHEN: the U-turn is fluent, he responds to the marker, and you can get 4-5 loose-leash steps in a row on a quiet street.

subtasks.title: Week 2: Engage-Disengage Level 1 at threshold distance
subtasks.description:
GOAL THIS WEEK: he can look at another dog and turn back to you for food, from far away. Nothing more ambitious than that.

FIND YOUR PRACTICE SPOT: somewhere dogs pass predictably at a distance you control - the far edge of a park, a bench across from a trail entrance, the edge of a supermarket car park. You need to be able to sit at 100+ feet and retreat further if needed.

FIND THE THRESHOLD DISTANCE: the distance at which he NOTICES another dog but does not bark. Write the number down in feet. That number is your progress metric for the whole month.

LEVEL 1 (ENGAGE), 3-4 sessions this week:
1. Stand at threshold distance. Be quiet and still. Let him notice the dog on his own - don't cue him.
2. The moment he LOOKS at the other dog, CLICK.
3. When he turns his head back to you after the click, feed.
4. If he reacts, or doesn't turn back after the click, you are too close. Move further away and reset.

Goal: 3-5 successful reps in a row at the same distance. A success = he turns back to you immediately after the click.
Session length: 1-5 minutes, then a break. Two or three short sessions beats one long one.
STOP if you see lip-licking, yawning, or scratching - those are stress signals, and you're over threshold.

Meanwhile: keep the avoid-dogs routing for all non-training walks. Continue 300-Peck loose leash on quiet streets, building to 8-10 steps.

READY FOR WEEK 3 WHEN: you've hit 3-5 clean reps in a row at the same distance, on more than one occasion.

subtasks.title: Week 3: Engage-Disengage Level 2, and start closing the distance
subtasks.description:
GOAL THIS WEEK: he chooses to look away from another dog on his own, and the working distance starts shrinking.

LEVEL 2 (DISENGAGE):
1. Let him notice the other dog, then WAIT 1-5 seconds - don't click the look this time. You're waiting to see if he'll look away by himself.
2. If he stares for more than 5 seconds, that's a fail: go back to Level 1 for a few reps.
3. The instant he DISENGAGES - looks away from the dog - CLICK, then feed.
4. If he reacts or won't turn back after the click, move further away and reset.

Goal: 3-5 successful reps in a row, THEN move 1-5 steps closer. Only a few steps. This is the week people rush and blow the whole month.
Rule to hold onto: if the other dog is moving or getting more intense, drop back to Level 1 at the new distance. Level 2 is for static or predictable triggers.

ON REAL WALKS: your emergency plan is now U-turn, or 'find it' scatter, whichever you can execute faster. Use it and leave - do not stand and try to train through a surprise encounter.

LOOSE LEASH: take the 300-Peck work to a slightly busier street, at a time of day with few dogs about. Expect to reset the count more often in a new place - that's normal, not a setback.

LOG IT: note the working distance in feet at the end of each session. If the number isn't trending down at all across the week, don't push harder - re-read the tripwires on the hire-vs-DIY subtask.

READY FOR WEEK 4 WHEN: he reliably self-interrupts and looks away, and you've closed the distance at least somewhat from the Week 2 number.

subtasks.title: Week 4: moving dogs, parallel passes, and an honest assessment
subtasks.description:
GOAL THIS WEEK: handle a dog that is MOVING, and decide what happens next.

MOVING TRIGGERS: a dog walking past is much harder than one standing still. Go back to Level 1 (click the look) at the distance where he can handle motion - which will be further away than your Week 3 static distance. That's expected, not a regression.

PARALLEL PASSES: if you can recruit a friend with a calm, non-reactive dog, walk in the same direction on opposite sides of a wide street or field, at your threshold distance, clicking and feeding throughout. Do NOT let them meet. No greetings, no 'saying hi'. This is the single highest-value exercise of the month if you can arrange it, and it's also exactly what a reactive-dog class supplies on tap.

REALISTIC 4-WEEK TARGET: pass a dog on the far side of a normal residential street without a bark, on a loose leash, taking food throughout. That is a genuine result at four weeks. What you should NOT expect yet: passing dogs on the same narrow pavement, handling a lunging or barking dog coming the other way, or anything at all at a dog park.

ASSESS AND DECIDE:
1. Compare this week's working distance in feet against the Week 2 number. Is it trending down?
2. Any of the tripwires appeared? (bite, unmanageable lunging, no progress at all, reactivity generalising, can't recover after an incident, refusing food outdoors) - if yes, book a private behaviour consult or a vet behaviourist rather than continuing solo.
3. If progress is real but slow: that's the normal case, and it's the argument for enrolling in the reactive-dog group class for the controlled setups.

Then keep going. Four weeks is the start of this, not the end - expect a few months to a solid result.
